newsitem.title: USA: GOLF - TIGER WOODS - A MICHAEL JORDAN IN THE MAKING.
newsitem.headline: GOLF - TIGER WOODS - A MICHAEL JORDAN IN THE MAKING.

text.p: Twenty-year-old Tiger Woods, unquestionably the hottest new golfer to come along in years, is on track to become the next superstar of sports marketing as well, experts say.

His professional career less than one month old, Woods is seen taking away as much as $150 million over the next five years, and eventually rivaling the the biggest money maker of all, basketball superstar Michael Jordan.

Woods, who won an unprecedented third consecutive U.S. Amateur championship this summer, already has contracts worth $60 million, which includes a five-year deal with Nike Corp. for $8 million a year.
But that is clearly just the beginning.

"Although golf is a much smaller game than basketball," says Roberto Muller, president of the Muller Sports Group, a New York sports marketing company that represents Magic Johnson, "Tiger can be as big as Michael Jordan as a sports celebrity figure.

"He has that great amateur record. He's cool. He's got a great smile. And he plays golf like he enjoys it and like Andre Agassi used to play tennis. All that makes him a marketing star. The big national brands like to play with the big stars."

Woods already has proven his "star" power -- attracting record crowds to the Amateur championship in Oregon in July and helping it draw a far bigger television audience than the one watching the PGA Tour event televised at the same time.
The former star of the Stanford University golf team also attracted enormous crowds at the Milwaukee Open last month when he played his first tournament as a professional.
While he did not seriously challenge for the title in that event, Woods still garnered the biggest galleries of the week, with crowds six-deep lining every hole he played.

And he did not disappoint his growing legions of fans. He consistently hit the ball farther than anyone else -- even the famous long-hitting John Daly -- and he capped his pro debut with a hole in one on Sunday.

In addition, the novelty of a man of colour -- his father is African-American and his mother is Thai -- participating in the almost totally white world of professional golf adds to his marketing appeal.

"Even Tiger Woods' name is just right for product endorsements," observes Darci Ross, president of CMG Worldwide, marketing and rights protection company in Minneapolis, which represents the estate of Jackie Robinson, who broke professional baseball's colour barrier in 1947.

"'Woods' denotes golf clubs," she said. "And there's the thrust of the Tiger name. He's young and appeals to the young. But he has won the amateur title for three years running so that even older people, and a lot of golfers are older, can identify with him. I think that Tiger's marketing potential is far greater than that of Jack Nicklaus," she said.
The daughter of a golf pro, Ross believes that the young golfer has the quiet, confident charisma that will allow him to cross over to other fields unrelated to golf as a celebrity endorser.

"When Jack Nicklaus started out, his marketing potential was much less than Tiger's is today," she said. "He (Woods) could do Gatorade, automobiles, cereal, whatever. He has a fantastic, marketing potential. He could hit $150 million."
However, some see Tiger's great monetary potential as a possible trap that could hurt his credibility.
"He has to be concerned that he doesn't overcommit and overexpose himself," noted Jeff Klein, a partner in the New York law firm of Weil, Gotshal and Manges.

The agent for former baseball star Dave Winfield, Klein said: "At this stage, with the Nike contract in hand, I can't imagine that money is a big factor. I understand, too, that the Nike contract is guaranteed, meaning that it will continue over the five years irrespective of Tiger's performance."

Sport celebrities' images are "only as good as the worst commercial that they have," he added. "They could have six commercials but people will remember them for the one that did not fit, the one that they seemed out of sorts with."
In Tiger Woods' case, Klein continued, "The special elements are his spirit, his drive, his earnestness, which are partly due to the limited access he has given of himself to endorsements.
"He and the people who guide him have to ask themselves if any new endorsements represent a product that he uses. Is there a natural association between him and that product?
"Dave Winfield turned down a very big hot-dog promotion deal because he didn't feel right pushing the product. He also turned down a company making a soda that he doesn't drink."
Klein said his advice to Tiger Woods "is to go slowly and avoid the temptation to take on so much that he will become overexposed.

"He should make sure that he doesn't become thought of as a commodity who pitches products and happens to be a golfer. Right now, people like him. He is appealing. He should be careful not to change that."
